rows.name: Iron Pagoda of Youguo Temple completed
rows.desc: The brick pagoda clad in iron-coloured glazed tiles was finished in the northeast of Kaifeng, replacing a wooden pagoda lost to lightning.

rows.name: Death of Fan Zhongyan
rows.desc: The reformer of the Qingli era died at Xuzhou while travelling to a new post.

rows.name: Title Duke Yansheng created for Confucius's heir
rows.desc: Emperor Renzong gave Kong Zongyuan, the senior descendant of Confucius at Qufu, the new hereditary title Duke Yansheng.

rows.name: Di Qing heads the Bureau of Military Affairs
rows.desc: The general who rose from the ranks served as military affairs commissioner at court until civil officials had him removed.

rows.name: Death of Di Qing
rows.desc: Di Qing died at Chenzhou, the prefecture to which he had been sent after losing his court post.

rows.name: Bao Zheng as prefect of Kaifeng
rows.desc: The incorruptible official later celebrated as Judge Bao governed the capital prefecture and let petitioners approach his court directly.

rows.name: Death of Bao Zheng
rows.desc: Bao Zheng died in the capital while serving as vice commissioner of military affairs.

rows.name: Jinshi examination of 1057
rows.desc: With Ouyang Xiu as chief examiner, the capital examination passed Su Shi, Su Zhe, Zeng Gong, Zhang Zai and Cheng Hao in a single year.

rows.name: Su Xun in the capital
rows.desc: Su Xun brought his sons Su Shi and Su Zhe from Sichuan to Kaifeng and won fame there for his essays.

rows.name: Death of Su Xun
rows.desc: Su Xun died in Kaifeng after working on a compilation of court ritual.

rows.name: Wang Anshi's Myriad Word Memorial
rows.desc: Wang Anshi submitted a long memorial to Emperor Renzong arguing for a thorough reform of government and of how officials were trained.

rows.name: Death of Mei Yaochen
rows.desc: The poet Mei Yaochen, a friend of Ouyang Xiu, died in Kaifeng during an epidemic.

rows.name: New Book of Tang presented
rows.desc: Ouyang Xiu and Song Qi presented their revised official history of the Tang dynasty to the throne.

rows.name: Han Qi as chief councillor
rows.desc: Han Qi led the government through the successions of Yingzong and Shenzong.

rows.name: Death of Emperor Renzong
rows.desc: Renzong, the longest-reigning Northern Song emperor, died in the palace after forty-one years on the throne.

rows.name: Yongzhao Mausoleum for Renzong
rows.desc: Renzong was buried in the imperial cemetery at Gongyi, between Kaifeng and Luoyang.

rows.name: Accession of Emperor Yingzong
rows.desc: Renzong's adopted heir Zhao Shu took the throne, with Empress Dowager Cao briefly sharing power.

rows.name: Puyi controversy
rows.desc: Court officials split bitterly over what ritual title Yingzong should give his natural father, Prince Pu.

rows.name: Death of Emperor Yingzong
rows.desc: Yingzong died after a short reign and was succeeded by his son Zhao Xu, Emperor Shenzong.

rows.name: Ouyang Xiu prefect of Bozhou
rows.desc: After leaving the court Ouyang Xiu governed Bozhou on his way to retirement.

rows.name: Accession of Emperor Shenzong
rows.desc: The nineteen-year-old Shenzong came to the throne determined to strengthen the state's finances and army.

rows.name: Wang Anshi leads the reform government
rows.desc: Wang Anshi became assistant councillor in 1069 and chief councillor in 1070, with a break in 1074 to 1075, and ran Shenzong's reforms.

rows.name: Finance Planning Commission set up
rows.desc: A new office was created at court to draft the fiscal laws of the New Policies outside the old finance bureaucracy.

rows.name: Green Sprouts law
rows.desc: The state began lending grain and cash to farmers in spring, to be repaid with interest at harvest.

rows.name: Equitable Transport law
rows.desc: Transport intendants were allowed to buy tribute goods where they were cheapest and to sell surplus, to cut the cost of supplying the capital.

rows.name: Baojia mutual security system
rows.desc: Rural households were grouped into units responsible for policing and later militia training, beginning around the capital.

rows.name: Hired Service law
rows.desc: Compulsory local service duties were replaced by a graduated cash levy used to hire workers.

rows.name: Poetry dropped from the examinations
rows.desc: Wang Anshi's reform replaced the poetry composition in the jinshi examination with essays on the classics and policy.

rows.name: Three Halls system at the Imperial University
rows.desc: The Imperial University in Kaifeng was reorganised into graded Outer, Inner and Upper halls through which students could be promoted.

rows.name: State Trade law
rows.desc: A Market Exchange Bureau in Kaifeng bought up goods from merchants and made loans, aiming to break the hold of large dealers.

rows.name: Land survey and equitable tax
rows.desc: A cadastral survey graded land by quality so that tax could be assessed more fairly, starting in the north.

rows.name: Horse-raising law
rows.desc: Northern households were given government horses to raise for the cavalry in return for tax relief.

rows.name: Guild service commuted to cash
rows.desc: Kaifeng's merchant guilds were allowed to pay a money fee instead of supplying goods to government offices on demand.

rows.name: Lü Huiqing at court
rows.desc: Wang Anshi's chief lieutenant ran the reform government during his first absence, then fell out with him.

rows.name: Guo Xi at the imperial painting academy
rows.desc: The landscape painter Guo Xi was Shenzong's favourite court artist and painted screens for palace halls.

rows.name: Early Spring by Guo Xi
rows.desc: Guo Xi painted his monumental hanging scroll of mountains emerging from mist, dated 1072.

rows.name: Shen Kuo in the capital
rows.desc: Shen Kuo directed the Bureau of Astronomy, served in the Hanlin Academy and headed the state finance commission.

rows.name: Shen Kuo surveys the Bian canal
rows.desc: Shen Kuo levelled the Bian canal between Kaifeng and the Huai with a series of dykes to measure its fall for dredging and silt-flushing works.

rows.name: Drought and famine in the north
rows.desc: A long drought drove refugees toward the capital and fed attacks on the New Policies.

rows.name: Zheng Xia's picture of refugees
rows.desc: A gate official sent the emperor a drawing of starving refugees blaming the reforms, which helped bring Wang Anshi's first resignation.

rows.name: New Interpretations of the Three Classics
rows.desc: Wang Anshi's official commentaries on the Odes, Documents and Rites of Zhou became the standard for the examinations.

rows.name: Death of Han Qi
rows.desc: The former chief councillor, an opponent of the Green Sprouts loans, died at his home prefecture of Xiangzhou.

rows.name: Death of Wang Pang
rows.desc: Wang Anshi's son and collaborator on the classics commentaries died young, and his father left office soon after.

rows.name: Sima Guang in Luoyang
rows.desc: Opposed to the New Policies, Sima Guang withdrew to Luoyang and spent fifteen years writing his chronicle of Chinese history.

rows.name: Garden of Solitary Enjoyment
rows.desc: Sima Guang laid out a small garden in Luoyang with a study where he worked on his history.

rows.name: Shao Yong in Luoyang
rows.desc: The cosmologist Shao Yong lived in modest retirement in his Nest of Peace and Happiness, a gathering place for Luoyang's scholars.

rows.name: Death of Shao Yong
rows.desc: Shao Yong died in Luoyang, mourned by Sima Guang and the Cheng brothers.

rows.name: Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi teaching in Luoyang
rows.desc: The Cheng brothers, out of favour under the reformers, taught the learning of principle in Luoyang.

rows.name: Luoyang society of venerable elders
rows.desc: Wen Yanbo gathered retired senior statesmen in Luoyang, including Fu Bi and Sima Guang, into a club of elders.

rows.name: Death of Fu Bi
rows.desc: The elder statesman, who had negotiated with the Liao in 1042, died in retirement at Luoyang.

rows.name: Birth of Zhao Xu, later Emperor Zhezong
rows.desc: Shenzong's sixth son, who would reign as Zhezong, was born in the palace.

rows.name: Yellow River breaks at Caocun
rows.desc: The Yellow River burst its dykes in Chanzhou and its waters spread south and east across dozens of counties.

rows.name: Su Shi prefect of Xuzhou
rows.desc: Su Shi governed Xuzhou, where he organised the city's defence against the 1077 flood.

rows.name: Xuzhou saved from the flood
rows.desc: With floodwater rising against the city walls, Su Shi stayed on the walls and had soldiers build an embankment until the waters fell.

rows.name: Yellow Tower built at Xuzhou
rows.desc: Su Shi built a tower on the east wall to mark the city's survival, painted yellow for the earth element that checks water.

rows.name: Coal found near Xuzhou
rows.desc: Coal was discovered southwest of Xuzhou and used to smelt iron, and Su Shi celebrated it in a poem.

rows.name: Luo River diverted into the Bian canal
rows.desc: To reduce Yellow River silt in Kaifeng's lifeline canal, clear water from the Luo River was led into the Bian.

rows.name: Crow Terrace Poetry Trial
rows.desc: Su Shi was arrested and tried by the Censorate for poems mocking the New Policies, then exiled to Huangzhou.

rows.name: Yellow River breaks at Xiaowu
rows.desc: Another breach in Chanzhou sent the river north, starting years of argument over whether to force it back east.

rows.name: Birth of Zhao Ji, later Emperor Huizong
rows.desc: Shenzong's eleventh son, the future artist emperor, was born in the palace.

rows.name: Zizhi Tongjian presented
rows.desc: Sima Guang completed and presented his 294-chapter chronicle covering 1,362 years of history, written mostly in Luoyang.

rows.name: Birth of Li Qingzhao
rows.desc: The greatest woman poet of the Song was born at Zhangqiu near Jinan to a scholar-official family.

rows.name: Death of Emperor Shenzong
rows.desc: Shenzong died at thirty-six, leaving the eight-year-old Zhezong under the regency of Empress Dowager Gao.

rows.name: Yongyu Mausoleum for Shenzong
rows.desc: Shenzong was buried in the imperial cemetery at Gongyi.

rows.name: Regency of Empress Dowager Gao
rows.desc: Shenzong's mother governed for Zhezong and recalled the conservative opponents of reform.

rows.name: Yuanyou repeal of the New Policies
rows.desc: Under Sima Guang the court abolished the Green Sprouts loans, the Hired Service levy and other reform laws.

rows.name: Sima Guang chief councillor
rows.desc: Summoned from Luoyang, Sima Guang led the government for the last months of his life.

rows.name: Death of Sima Guang
rows.desc: Sima Guang died in Kaifeng in office, months after Wang Anshi died in Jiangning.

rows.name: Su Shi at court in the Yuanyou years
rows.desc: Recalled from exile, Su Shi served as Hanlin academician and drafter of edicts, while quarrelling with both reformers and Cheng Yi's followers.

rows.name: Su Zhe at court
rows.desc: Su Shi's younger brother rose to assistant councillor under the Yuanyou regency.

rows.name: Cheng Yi lectures to the young emperor
rows.desc: Cheng Yi was appointed to lecture on the classics to Zhezong, but his strictness made enemies and he was soon removed.

rows.name: Huang Tingjian in Kaifeng
rows.desc: The poet and calligrapher worked on the Veritable Records of Shenzong's reign in the capital.

rows.name: Qin Guan in Kaifeng
rows.desc: Su Shi's disciple Qin Guan held posts in the imperial library and wrote his celebrated ci lyrics.

rows.name: Li Gonglin in Kaifeng
rows.desc: The scholar-painter, famous for fine-line figure and horse painting, spent much of his official career in the capital.

rows.name: Su Song's astronomical clock tower
rows.desc: Su Song and Han Gonglian built a water-driven tower with an armillary sphere, celestial globe and time-announcing figures in the palace.

rows.name: Xin Yixiang Fayao
rows.desc: Su Song's illustrated treatise described the construction of the clock tower and its escapement.

rows.name: Zhezong begins personal rule
rows.desc: The death of Empress Dowager Gao let the young emperor take power and turn against her ministers.

rows.name: Shaosheng restoration of the reforms
rows.desc: Zhezong proclaimed the Shaosheng era, restored the New Policies and sent Yuanyou officials such as Su Shi into far exile.

rows.name: Zhang Dun chief councillor
rows.desc: The reformer Zhang Dun led Zhezong's government and the purge of the conservatives.

rows.name: Death of Wen Yanbo
rows.desc: The long-lived statesman who had served four emperors died in Luoyang aged about ninety.

rows.name: Yellow River breach at Neihuang
rows.desc: The river broke through at Neihuang and abandoned its eastern channel for a northern course.

rows.name: Death of Emperor Zhezong
rows.desc: Zhezong died at twenty-three without a surviving son, and his brother Zhao Ji was chosen to succeed.

rows.name: Yongtai Mausoleum for Zhezong
rows.desc: Zhezong was the last emperor buried at the Gongyi imperial cemetery before the fall of the north.

rows.name: Accession of Emperor Huizong
rows.desc: Huizong took the throne with Empress Dowager Xiang briefly sharing power.

rows.name: Birth of Zhao Huan, later Emperor Qinzong
rows.desc: Huizong's eldest son, the last Northern Song emperor, was born in the palace.

rows.name: Li Qingzhao marries Zhao Mingcheng
rows.desc: The poet married a student of the Imperial University and the couple began collecting books and bronze and stone inscriptions in Kaifeng.

rows.name: Li Qingzhao in Kaifeng
rows.desc: Li Qingzhao lived in the capital in the first years of her marriage until factional purges drove the family away.

rows.name: Su Shi buried at Jia County
rows.desc: Su Shi, who died at Changzhou in 1101, was buried at Mount Xiao'e in Jia County, Henan, where his brother later joined him.

rows.name: Cai Jing dominates the government
rows.desc: Cai Jing served as chief councillor for most of Huizong's reign, with several dismissals and returns.

rows.name: Yuanyou faction blacklist stele
rows.desc: The names of Yuanyou officials, including Sima Guang and Su Shi, were carved on a stele at a palace gate and barred their families from office.

rows.name: Blacklist extended to 309 names
rows.desc: An enlarged list of 309 proscribed officials was carved and copies were set up in prefectures across the empire.

rows.name: Blacklist stele destroyed after a comet
rows.desc: Alarmed by a comet, Huizong ordered the faction stele smashed and eased the bans.

rows.name: Yingzao Fashi printed
rows.desc: Li Jie's state building manual, with standard modules and illustrated details for timber construction, was printed by imperial order.

rows.name: Li Jie at the Directorate of Buildings
rows.desc: Li Jie supervised state construction in the capital, including palaces and offices, and compiled the Yingzao Fashi.

rows.name: Birth of Yue Fei
rows.desc: The general who would fight the Jurchen was born to a farming family at Tangyin in Xiangzhou.

rows.name: Large ten-cash coins issued
rows.desc: Cai Jing's government issued heavy token coins worth ten ordinary cash, which caused inflation and counterfeiting.

rows.name: Jiaozi renamed qianyin
rows.desc: The court renamed the state paper money qianyin and extended it beyond Sichuan, but overissue soon made the notes lose value.

rows.name: School of painting set up
rows.desc: Huizong added a painting school to the state education system, examining students on poetic themes.

rows.name: State schools replace the examinations
rows.desc: Cai Jing suspended the prefectural examinations so that officials would be recruited through the graded school system instead.

rows.name: Poorhouses, clinics and paupers' cemeteries
rows.desc: Huizong's government ordered houses for the poor and aged, public clinics and cemeteries for the unclaimed dead in every prefecture.

rows.name: Mi Fu as professor of calligraphy and painting
rows.desc: The eccentric calligrapher and connoisseur held a post teaching painting and calligraphy in the capital.

rows.name: Nine Tripods cast
rows.desc: Huizong had nine ritual cauldrons cast for a new palace hall, along with new court music.

rows.name: Death of Cheng Yi
rows.desc: Cheng Yi died near Luoyang, his teaching still officially banned.

rows.name: Birth of Zhao Gou, later Emperor Gaozong
rows.desc: Huizong's ninth son, who would refound the dynasty in the south, was born in the palace.

rows.name: Auspicious Cranes
rows.desc: Huizong painted twenty cranes circling the palace gate, recording an omen seen at the Lantern Festival.

rows.name: Death of Su Zhe
rows.desc: Su Zhe died at Yingchang, where he had lived quietly in retirement after the purges.

rows.name: Su Zhe retired at Yingchang
rows.desc: Barred from office, Su Zhe lived his last years writing at Yingchang.

rows.name: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains
rows.desc: The teenage court painter Wang Ximeng finished his long blue-green landscape scroll under Huizong's instruction.
rows.wikipedia: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains

rows.name: Wang Ximeng at court
rows.desc: A student of the painting school, Wang Ximeng was trained personally by Huizong.

rows.name: Zhang Zeduan in Kaifeng
rows.desc: The painter of the Qingming scroll worked in the capital, probably in Huizong's painting academy.

rows.name: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
rows.desc: Zhang Zeduan's handscroll shows boats, a rainbow bridge, shops and crowds along the Bian River outside Kaifeng.
rows.wikipedia: Along the River During the Qingming Festival

rows.name: Zhou Bangyan heads the music bureau
rows.desc: The ci poet Zhou Bangyan directed the court office of music and refined the tunes used for lyric songs.

rows.name: Lin Lingsu at Huizong's court
rows.desc: The Daoist master won Huizong's favour by telling him he was the incarnation of a celestial lord of the Divine Empyrean.

rows.name: Genyue imperial garden
rows.desc: Huizong built an artificial mountain park in the northeast of Kaifeng, filled with rare rocks and plants shipped from the south.

rows.name: Flower and rock convoys
rows.desc: Agents seized rare stones and plants in the southeast and shipped them up the canal to Kaifeng, a hated burden on the people.

rows.name: Buddhist monasteries renamed as Daoist
rows.desc: Huizong ordered Buddhist clergy to take Daoist titles and dress, a measure soon reversed.

rows.name: Xuanhe Painting Catalogue
rows.desc: The palace compiled a catalogue of more than six thousand paintings in Huizong's collection, arranged by subject.

rows.name: Illustrated catalogue of antiquities
rows.desc: Huizong's court catalogued over eight hundred ancient bronzes in its collection with drawings and inscriptions.

rows.name: Wind in Pines Among a Myriad Valleys
rows.desc: Li Tang painted his towering landscape of pines and cliffs, inscribed with the date 1124.

rows.name: Li Tang in Huizong's academy
rows.desc: Li Tang worked as a court painter in Kaifeng before fleeing south after its fall.

rows.name: Alliance Conducted at Sea
rows.desc: Envoys travelling by sea agreed with the Jurchen Jin to attack the Liao together, with the Song to receive the Sixteen Prefectures.

rows.name: Tong Guan commands the armies
rows.desc: The palace eunuch Tong Guan held supreme military command and led the failed campaigns against the Liao.

rows.name: Song Jiang's band of outlaws
rows.desc: A band led by Song Jiang roamed the eastern circuits before surrendering, later remembered in the Water Margin as the heroes of Liangshan Marsh.

rows.name: First Patriarch's Hall at Shaolin
rows.desc: A stone and timber hall honouring Bodhidharma was built on the hill above Shaolin Monastery, one of the oldest buildings in Henan.

rows.name: Ru ware made for the court
rows.desc: Kilns at Qingliangsi in Ruzhou produced pale blue-green crackled stoneware for the palace for a few decades.

rows.name: Jun ware kilns at Yuzhou
rows.desc: Kilns around Yuzhou produced thick, opalescent blue glazes splashed with purple.

rows.name: Cizhou ware kilns
rows.desc: Kilns around Cizhou made everyday stoneware with bold black-on-white painted and carved designs for ordinary households.

rows.name: Xiangguo Temple market days
rows.desc: The courtyards of Daxiangguo Temple held a great market several days a month selling animals, household goods, books and antiques.

rows.name: Night market at Zhou Bridge
rows.desc: Food stalls along the imperial way near Zhou Bridge stayed open late into the night.

rows.name: Pleasure quarters and theatres
rows.desc: Kaifeng's entertainment quarters held dozens of enclosed stages where storytellers, puppeteers, acrobats and actors performed daily.

rows.name: Fan Tower wine house
rows.desc: The best known of the capital's great wine houses was rebuilt as five linked three-storey buildings joined by bridges.

rows.name: Lantern Festival before the palace
rows.desc: For the Lantern Festival huge lantern displays were built before the Xuande Gate and the emperor appeared before the crowds.

rows.name: Jinming Pool opened to the public
rows.desc: Each spring the imperial pool west of the city was opened for boat races, naval displays and picnics.

rows.name: Grain fleets on the Bian canal
rows.desc: Millions of bushels of tax grain came up the Bian canal from the Huai and Yangzi each year to feed the capital and its armies.

rows.name: Kaifeng outer wall rebuilt
rows.desc: Shenzong had the outer city wall of the capital heightened and rebuilt.

rows.name: Daxiangguo Temple, the great state monastery
rows.desc: The richest Buddhist monastery of the capital housed many cloisters and hosted state ceremonies.

rows.name: Songyang Academy
rows.desc: The old academy at the foot of Mount Song was one of the famous academies of the Northern Song and is linked with the Cheng brothers' teaching.

rows.name: Yingtian Academy at the Southern Capital
rows.desc: The academy at Yingtian prefecture, where Fan Zhongyan had taught, was one of the four great academies of the Song.

rows.name: Zeng Gong prefect of Qizhou
rows.desc: The essayist Zeng Gong governed Qizhou, the later Jinan, suppressing banditry and improving its lakes and waterworks.

rows.name: Su Zhe at Chenzhou
rows.desc: After opposing the reforms Su Zhe served as a prefectural school instructor at Chenzhou.

rows.name: Jin armies invade the Song
rows.desc: After destroying the Liao, the Jurchen Jin turned on their Song allies, sending two armies south toward Kaifeng.

rows.name: Huizong abdicates
rows.desc: As the Jin army approached, Huizong handed the throne to his son Qinzong and soon fled south.

rows.name: Jin cavalry crosses the Yellow River
rows.desc: Wanyan Zongwang's army crossed the Yellow River near Huazhou almost unopposed after Song defenders fled.

rows.name: First Jin siege of Kaifeng
rows.desc: Li Gang organised the defence of the capital and the Jin withdrew after Qinzong promised a huge indemnity and three northern prefectures.

rows.name: Li Gang defends the capital
rows.desc: Li Gang led the defence of Kaifeng and argued against concessions until he was sent away from court.

rows.name: Chen Dong's student protest
rows.desc: Imperial University student Chen Dong led a huge crowd to the palace gate demanding Li Gang's recall and punishment of the officials blamed for the crisis.

rows.name: Huizong flees to the south
rows.desc: The retired emperor left Kaifeng by the canal for Bozhou and the Yangzi, returning after the first siege ended.

rows.name: Zhao Gou's headquarters at Xiangzhou
rows.desc: Prince Kang was named marshal of the Hebei armies and gathered troops at Xiangzhou instead of relieving the capital.

rows.name: Second Jin siege of Kaifeng
rows.desc: Both Jin armies converged on Kaifeng and surrounded the city in winter.

rows.name: Fall of Kaifeng
rows.desc: Jin troops took the city walls and Qinzong went to the Jin camp to surrender.

rows.name: Kaifeng stripped of treasure
rows.desc: The Jin demanded vast amounts of gold, silver and silk and carried off books, ritual vessels, printing blocks and astronomical instruments.

rows.name: Zhang Bangchang made emperor of Chu
rows.desc: The Jin installed the former Song chancellor as ruler of a puppet state of Chu, which he gave up within weeks of their departure.

rows.name: Jingkang incident: emperors taken north
rows.desc: Huizong, Qinzong and thousands of members of the imperial clan, palace women and craftsmen were marched into captivity in the north.

rows.name: End of the Northern Song
rows.desc: The capture of the emperors ended the Northern Song period and Kaifeng's role as the Song capital.

rows.name: Zhao Gou enthroned at Yingtian
rows.desc: Prince Kang was proclaimed emperor at the Southern Capital, Yingtian prefecture, beginning the Southern Song.

rows.name: Li Gang chief councillor at Yingtian
rows.desc: Gaozong appointed Li Gang chief councillor, then dismissed him after about seventy-five days.

rows.name: Execution of Chen Dong
rows.desc: Chen Dong was executed at Gaozong's court for protesting Li Gang's dismissal, and was rehabilitated soon after.

rows.name: Zong Ze holds Kaifeng
rows.desc: The veteran official Zong Ze was made governor of Kaifeng, rebuilt its defences and rallied volunteer armies against the Jin.

rows.name: Meng Yuanlao in Kaifeng
rows.desc: The minor official who later wrote the Dongjing Meng Hua Lu, a memoir of the capital's streets, food and festivals, lived in the city in these years.

rows.name: Chen Dong at the Imperial University
rows.desc: Chen Dong came to study at the Imperial University in Kaifeng and became a leader of student opinion.

rows.name: Empress Dowager Xiang shares power
rows.desc: Shenzong's widow briefly co-ruled with Huizong and recalled some Yuanyou officials.

rows.name: Shenzong orders the Western Xia campaign
rows.desc: The court in Kaifeng launched a five-pronged offensive against the Tangut Western Xia, which ended in costly failure in 1082.

rows.name: Zhao Mingcheng at the Imperial University
rows.desc: Li Qingzhao's husband studied and served in Kaifeng and began the collection catalogued in his Records on Metal and Stone.

rows.name: Kaifeng, largest city of its age
rows.desc: The Song capital on the Bian canal held perhaps a million people within and around its three rings of walls.

rows.name: Fan Pagoda, Kaifeng
rows.desc: The tile-faced brick pagoda of the Tianqing Temple, built in 974, stood in the southeast of the capital.

rows.name: Su Shi's ci lyrics at Xuzhou
rows.desc: At Xuzhou Su Shi wrote poems on farming villages and rain prayers, widening the subjects of the ci lyric.

rows.name: Famine and epidemic in besieged Kaifeng
rows.desc: During the Jin occupation food ran out, prices soared and many residents died of hunger and disease.

rows.name: Wen Yanbo in Luoyang
rows.desc: The senior statesman lived in retirement in Luoyang, apart from a return to court in 1086.

rows.name: Zhang Zai lectures in the capital
rows.desc: Before passing the jinshi, Zhang Zai lectured on the Book of Changes in Kaifeng and met his nephews the Cheng brothers.

rows.name: Failed diversion of the Yellow River
rows.desc: An attempt to close the river's northern channel and send it back to an old eastern course collapsed, drowning many people.

rows.name: Wang Anshi's first dismissal
rows.desc: Wang Anshi left the chief councillorship for Jiangning and was recalled a year later.

rows.name: Wang Anshi's final retirement
rows.desc: Wang Anshi resigned for good and retired to Jiangning, though Shenzong kept the reforms going.

rows.name: Genyue garden torn apart
rows.desc: During the winter siege, residents of starving Kaifeng broke up Huizong's garden for firewood and food.
